claims.text: ACE sets the incline bench at 45-60 degrees; the Human Kinetics technique text uses about 45 degrees.

quotes.text: lie supine (on your back) on an incline bench angled between 45 and 60 degrees with your feet placed firmly on the floor or on a raised platform to allow you to maintain a neutral spine
In this variation, the back pad of the bench is set at an upward angle (approximately 45 degrees).

claims.text: In EMG studies of the barbell bench press, the upper chest peaked at a 30-degree incline, inclines above 45 degrees shifted work to the front deltoid and reduced chest performance, and triceps activity was similar at all inclines (barbell data applied to dumbbells).

quotes.text: The results showed that the maximal EMG activity for PMUP occurred at a bench inclination of 30°.
Inclinations greater than 45° produce significantly higher activation of the anterior deltoid and decrease the muscular performance of the pectoralis major.
TB showed similar EMG activities at all bench inclinations.

claims.text: Grip: closed, palms forward, thumbs wrapped; wrists neutral.

quotes.text: Grasp each dumbbell with a closed, pronated grip (palms facing forward, thumbs wrapped around the handle)
Maintain a neutral wrist position (avoid flexion / extension at the wrist joint).

claims.text: Shoulder blades down and back; head, shoulders, buttocks and feet keep contact.

quotes.text: Depress and retract your scapulae (pull shoulders down and back) to make firm contact with the bench. Your head, shoulders, butt and feet should make contact with the bench and floor/riser throughout the exercise.

claims.text: At lockout the elbows are fully extended with the dumbbells at eye level or slightly higher (ACE). The card uses this for height only and draws the dumbbells over the shoulders (c17).

quotes.text: press the dumbbells in unison to a level over your eyes or slightly higher, with your elbows fully extended

claims.text: Lower slowly toward the upper chest, slightly wide toward the armpits, touching gently without bouncing.

quotes.text: Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells in unison and in a controlled movement towards your upper chest, but moving slightly wider towards the armpits. Gently touch the dumbbells to your chest without bouncing
The lifter will lower the dumbbells to the top of their chest and then extend the elbows, pressing straight up.

claims.text: Keep the elbows under the wrists.

quotes.text: Keep the elbows under your wrists, and either close to your sides (emphasizes more triceps) or flared out from the body (emphasizes more pectorals).

claims.text: Avoid arching the low back; keep all contact points.

quotes.text: Maintain all points of contact with the bench and floor/riser and avoid any arching in the low back.

claims.text: Getting in: dumbbells on the thighs as you sit, then use the thighs to help lift them to shoulder height as you lie back.

quotes.text: Select a pair of dumbbells and place them on your thighs as you sit on the bench.
Sit back on the bench, and use your thighs to help lift the dumbbells to shoulder height.

claims.text: A way out: the spotter grips the lifter's wrists and takes the dumbbells one at a time at the end; the same spotting rules apply on the incline.

quotes.text: The spotter should place a firm grip with each hand around the wrists of the lifter. Spotting at the elbows is incorrect
All other positions and movement cues are similar.

claims.text: Breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.

quotes.text: Exhale and gently press upwards to full elbow extension with the dumbbells positioned at your starting position.

claims.text: At 30 and 45 degrees the upper chest was more active than flat during part of the press; a flat bench works both upper and lower chest (barbell study, applied to dumbbells).

quotes.text: The results of this study support the use of a horizontal bench to achieve muscular activation of both the upper and lower heads of the pectoralis.
a bench incline angle of 30° or 45° resulted in greater muscular activation during certain time points

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: ACSM recommends a moderate speed for strength work: 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Across US emergency-department weight-training injuries, the most common mechanism was weights dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: The shoulder is one of the most often injured areas in resistance training (up to 36% of documented injuries), and poor attention to technique is a named risk factor.

quotes.text: The results of the review indicated that up to 36% of documented RT-related injuries and disorders occur at the shoulder complex.
extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique
The shoulder complex in particular has been alluded to as one of the most prevalent regions of injury.

claims.text: Human Kinetics starts the dumbbell press with the dumbbells over the shoulders and says the incline version keeps the flat press's other positions and cues.

quotes.text: Lean back into a supine position on the bench while positioning your hands and dumbbells over your shoulders.
All other positions and movement cues are similar.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; bench angle, elbow-under-wrist and back arch all read in the sagittal plane (c1, c7, c8).
plate.equipment: Adjustable bench at 45 degrees (the value inside both ACE's 45-60 range and HK's 'about 45', c1; c2 notes 30 degrees peaks upper chest in barbell data, so 45 is the upper sensible limit). Dumbbell per hand, feet flat.
plate.start: On the incline, head/shoulders/buttocks on the pad, feet on the floor (c4); arms straight and vertical, dumbbells directly above the shoulder joints (c17, c7), so they sit above eye height (c5) and in front of the face, never over it.
plate.end: Dumbbells at the upper chest, slightly wide (c6), elbows under the wrists (c7).

checkpoints.label: Bench at 45°
checkpoints.what: Back pad at about 45 degrees; steeper shifts work to the front shoulder (barbell data).

checkpoints.label: Elbows under wrists
checkpoints.what: Forearms stay vertical under the dumbbells.

checkpoints.label: To upper chest
checkpoints.what: Dumbbells come down to the top of the chest, slightly wide.

mistake.what: Elbows drifting out of line with the wrists (forearms tilted) at the bottom.
mistake.why: ACE's only incline-specific cue is elbows under wrists; frequency is not measured in any source read.

grip.width: Dumbbells over the elbows, elbows under the wrists (c7).
grip.handContact: Handle held firmly in the palm (c3).

setup.step: Set the bench to about 45 degrees.
Sit with the dumbbells on your thighs.
Lie back, using your thighs to help lift the dumbbells to shoulder height.
Shoulder blades down and back; feet flat.
Press to straight arms, dumbbells over the shoulders.

posture.point: Head, shoulders, buttocks and feet keep contact.

handlingMistakes.fix: Lower the back pad; steeper shifts work to the front shoulder (barbell data).
Touch gently; go lighter if you can't.
Stop the set or go lighter.

rows.where: Mostly front of the shoulders, little chest
rows.means: Usually the bench is too steep.
rows.fix: Lower the bench to about 45 degrees or less.

rows.where: Sharp pain at the front of the shoulder
rows.means: Usually a warning sign; the shoulder is one of the most often injured areas in lifting.
rows.fix: Stop the set. Go lighter next time.

risks.risk: Weights dropping on the lifter is the most common weight-room injury mechanism; use a spotter for heavy sets.
Shoulder injuries are common in lifting and linked to poor technique.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json: upper_chest primary; front_delts, triceps, chest secondary. c2 supports upper_chest and front_delts, and triceps (Rodríguez-Ridao: similar triceps activity at all inclines, barbell data); c12 supports chest. No change.
